extracted.intended_audience: NIH leadership (DDER/CSR), study section members, program officers, grant reviewers, and researchers interested in peer review policy and evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and analyzing experiments and statistics to assess the reliability, validity, and bias of NIH grant peer review (study sections, reviewer composition, modalities, and post-review outcomes). Focused on proposals for CSR/NIH extramural review reform and validation studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test-retest reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Find out first if there is any problem with the reliability of review for proposals. Take an allocation of grants for a given study section and convene a parallel section with approximately the same sorts of folks. Or get really creative and split the original panels in half and fill in the rest with ad hocs. Whenever there is a SEP convened, put two or more of them together. Find out the degree to which the same grants get fundable scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convene parallel/replicate reviews of the identical pile of applications (preferably simultaneously) to measure whether the same grants are judged fundable. Use split-panels or duplicate panels; compare fundable/non-fundable classifications. Ensure analyses quantify agreement (not just anecdotes). Simultaneous review preferred to avoid contamination by time-dependent events (new papers, awards).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: INTER-RATER RELIABILITY. Measure how consistent different reviewers are when scoring the same applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess variability across individual reviewers and compute inter-rater agreement statistics (e.g., ICC, kappa). Use multiple reviewers/panels to determine within-panel and between-panel variability. Analyze whether reviewer disagreement affects funding decisions (e.g., wide score spread leading to triage vs discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of parallel/replicate study sections for validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever there is a SEP convened, put two or more of them together. Or split the original panels in half and fill in the rest with ad hocs. Whenever there is a SEP convened, put two or more of them together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational recommendation for implementing test-retest and inter-rater studies: explicitly create parallel study sections (or designate some panels as experimental replicates). Fill with representative reviewers/ad-hocs to mirror real panels. Can be CSR-run projects to avoid external contamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel composition effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Start convening parallel study sections to, again, review the exact same pile of grants except this time change the composition to see how reviewer characteristics may affect outcome. Make women-heavy panels, URM-heavy panels, panels dominated by the smaller University affiliations and/or less-active research programs, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically vary reviewer demographics and institutional affiliations to detect bias or systematic effects. Compare outcomes across differently composed panels to identify influence of reviewer characteristics on scores and funding rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare review modalities (face-to-face vs phone vs web-forum)
rubrics_metrics.description: They should review an identical pile of proposals in traditional face-to-face meetings versus phone-conference versus that horrible web-forum thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run controlled comparisons of deliberation modes using identical application sets to determine how modality influences scoring and discussion. Measure differences in scores, consensus, and fundable classifications across modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate effectiveness of blinding
rubrics_metrics.description: *And by the way, when testing out peer review, make sure to evaluate the blinding. You have to ask the reviewers to say who they think the PIs are, their level of confidence, etc. And you have to actually analyze the results intelligently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In blinded-review experiments, ask reviewers to guess applicant identities and report confidence. Analyze not only overall accuracy but the distribution of correct/erroneous guesses (test whether errors are random or patterned). Do not rely on a single statement like 'they missed most of the time' — check whether correct/incorrect guesses cluster by PI type, institution, or other features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report broader score statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: They propose reporting broader score statistics...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish fuller distributions and summary statistics of scores (not just paylines or means) so stakeholders can see variability, dispersion, and tails. Use comprehensive reporting to inform validity and reliability analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score renewals and new applications in separate panels
rubrics_metrics.description: Scoring renewals and new applications in separate panels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating different application types (e.g., renewals vs new R01s) in the same evaluation stream; consider separate review tracks/panels to reduce bias introduced by past performance signals and to allow cleaner measurement of reviewer judgment on distinct application types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlate scores with later outcome measures (predictive validity)
rubrics_metrics.description: They propose ... correlating scores with later outcome measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure predictive validity by linking review scores to subsequent objective outcomes (publications, citation impact, downstream grants). When possible include unfunded and just-missed applications to avoid selection bias. Use longitudinal tracking and normalized metrics (e.g., citation impact per dollar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selection bias and range truncation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no point in asking if peer review predicts X, Y or Z outcome for a given grant when funded if it cannot even predict itself in terms of what will get funded. It is madness that they continue to try to advance these as if they are meaningful! we need to know about the stuff that didn't get funded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not condition analyses solely on funded grants (range truncation). Include triaged and unfunded applications and 'just missed' cases in analyses. Design studies to capture the full distribution of applications to measure true predictive power of review scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for temporal confounds (simultaneous review)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best way is to have them reviewed simultaneously. otherwise it could be that a paper published or another grant awarded in between the reviews could contaminate things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing reviews, perform simultaneous or near-simultaneous reviews of identical application sets to minimize contamination from time-dependent events (publications, awards, career changes). If simultaneous review is impossible, carefully model and adjust for time-related covariates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical and procedural safeguards (confidentiality, informed consent, fairness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review is confidential. Review outcome is not known to the reviewers. They wouldn't have to know if they were in the 'real' one or not. ... Is it fair for future applicants to deal with a more flawed system just because the current crop of applicants can't deal with a delay? Imagine how pissed off the applicants are going to be when they find out they got scored well in one study section but are not funded or that their proposal that they agonized over for weeks/months was used in an experiment without their knowledge? Also, imagine how pissed off the reviewers are going to be when they find out that were part of an experiment and that all the effort that they put into reviewing was for naught if they scored an application very well but the other study sections didn't and it wasn't funded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for consent, confidentiality, and fairness when designing experimental validation. Consider whether to inform reviewers/applicants (informed consent) versus preserving natural behavior. Plan how to decide which panel's scores determine funding to avoid unfair harm to applicants. Consider CSR-only projects to limit leaks; weigh potential reviewer/applicant backlash and reviewer retention risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designate decision rule for experiments (which review 'counts')
rubrics_metrics.description: Speaking of which, no reason CSR can't assign one review panel as the one that counts and still convene other panels. The NIPS example had double review (to test for inter-evaluator reliability) and used the more positive review to determine outcome. I don't think that would work for grants ... but it would be easy to do the experiment while designating one of the two sections as the decision maker for each grant (while reviewers remained blind to that designation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-specify how funding decisions will be made in experiment contexts (e.g., designate one panel as the official decision-maker, use a tie-breaker rule, or use the more positive review). Choose rules that minimize unfair disadvantage to applicants and are ethically defensible; document decision rules publicly or to affected parties as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect and analyze reviewer-level scoring statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Do they keep track of individual reviewer statistics (e.g. scores given for each criteria)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track granular reviewer behavior (scores on each criterion, tendencies, variance) to identify systematic leniency/harshness, bias, or changes over time. Use reviewer-level metrics in reliability and bias modeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage existing multi-stage review designs for reliability estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: BTW many of the test you suggest are de rigeur in NSF/BIO. Each project comes in as a preliminary proposal, and the successful ones after review are evaluated by a different panel + ad hoc reviewers. In as much as one can trust that a preliminary proposal and a full proposal are similar, one can look for test-retest reliability and perhaps even inter-rater reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use staged review processes (pre-proposal/full-proposal) where different panels review different stages to estimate reliability and reproducibility. Borrow lessons and methods from other agencies (e.g., NSF) that already run multi-stage reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent publication and interpretation of results (avoid suppression)
rubrics_metrics.description: When important information is not available it is often because leaders are afraid to know the answers: so they either do not pose the necessary questions, or they repress results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for transparent reporting of validation experiment results regardless of outcomes. Pre-register studies or analytic plans where feasible to reduce suppression of unfavorable findings. Anticipate political and institutional consequences and prepare communication strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of practical/logistical constraints and reviewer supply
rubrics_metrics.description: The hardest part of DMs proposal is getting enough reviewers to pull it off, but having the pool be representative of the people that actually take the time and effort to sit on study section. Of course, if the NIH would just grow a pair and demand that any NIH-funded investigator can be called up to review once a year, this wouldn't be an issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess feasibility: reviewer recruitment, time and cost of extra reviews, frequency of panel meetings, and incentives. Consider using existing panels opportunistically (e.g., during budget delays) or funding special validation projects (e.g., ARRA-era experiments). Balance representativeness with practical limits.
